extracted.intended_audience: NPR listeners/readers interested in politics and investigative journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practices for investigative reporters re‑examining fast‑moving allegations about public figures, including how to gather facts, corroborate accounts, and balance fairness with public scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rushing to judgment / get the facts first
rubrics_metrics.description: "it was a mistake to rush to judgment without getting the facts first."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece emphasizes that decisions (including calls for resignation) made very quickly can be mistaken; reporters and officials should take time to assemble and verify evidence before concluding. Example: Franken's situation unfolded "within three weeks" from first allegation to resignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a formal ethics inquiry when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: "Senator Franken had wanted an ethics inquiry into the allegations and that never happened."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formal investigation/hearing (e.g., Ethics Committee) can surface facts and provide procedural fairness that ad hoc public pressure may not; reporters should note whether such institutional inquiries occurred or were bypassed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek corroboration and fact-check accusers
rubrics_metrics.description: "she had never been subjected to any fact-checking. She had never produced any corroborators."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should verify key claims, look for corroborating witnesses or evidence, and disclose when such corroboration is absent. Jane Mayer cites speaking to multiple tour members who did not corroborate the principal accuser's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take a 'second look' at cases that were quickly resolved
rubrics_metrics.description: "take a second look at the case, since Al Franken had never gotten the Ethics Committee investigation and hearing that he asked for."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative reexamination can clarify facts in controversies that were rapidly adjudicated in the court of public opinion; reporters may re-interview participants and examine overlooked evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to all sides / interview multiple perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: "just do the reporting, talk to all sides, put out the facts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balanced reporting requires speaking with accusers, the accused, neutral witnesses, and relevant officials to present a fuller picture and avoid one‑sided narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the facts guide the story / maintain open-mindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: "approach it with an open mind and to let the facts sort of guide me to where things are - you know, where it makes sense, where the truth seems to lie."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should avoid preconceived conclusions and follow evidence wherever it leads, even if it complicates prevailing narratives; this is presented as core investigative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for pushback on sensitive reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: "we were sort of poking a stick in the hornet's nest... it's a very touchy issue and a really important conversation in the country, but it's very inflamed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage that revisits contentious #MeToo-era cases will attract criticism; reporters should anticipate and be ready to defend methodology and sourcing, and recognize that many critics may not have read the full reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proportionality, due process, and fairness in #MeToo coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: "for the #MeToo movement to not be turned into something trivial, it's important that it keep in mind proportionality and due process and fairness and take into account the context of the various kinds of allegations that are being made."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Debra Katz, the transcript argues that movements and coverage should balance believing survivors with ensuring proportional, fair treatment of accused individuals and attention to contextual differences among allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize neutral eyewitness testimony when available
rubrics_metrics.description: "I spoke to eight people on that USO tour who had no political agenda... they just didn't see it the way she saw it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutral or nonpartisan eyewitnesses can be particularly valuable corroborators or counters to charged claims; reporters should seek such testimony and report its presence or absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge incomplete facts and transparently report limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: "We don't still have all of the facts because not every witness was willing to speak up."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reporting should be transparent about gaps in information, unwilling witnesses, and unresolved questions rather than overstating certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance timeliness with thoroughness
rubrics_metrics.description: The account notes the speed of events: "It all happened very, very fast. It all happened within three weeks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an implicit criterion to weigh the pressure to act quickly (or to publish) against the need for careful verification; rushing can lead to later reassessments or regrets by decision‑makers.
